report:
Answer: build INF-16 as six pieces. It cannot be one change because the work ships through three separate gates: a Mac alpha, builds on the captain's phone (Xcode, then TestFlight), and App Review, which also waits for counsel and the public pages. The captain's saved answers on 976b2359 all stay as chosen.

The six pieces, with what each needs merged first:
1. Your Mac lets a phone join as a phone. The join request takes an optional system. A phone joins as a view whichever link it used, so it is never listed under Runs on. While a phone is on the Mac's list, the Mac announces itself over Bonjour so the phone can find it again. Checks: pairing tests, a stand-in phone in the devices journey, the announcement test, and the contract file regenerated. Needs nothing. Why apart: pairing decides who may control the Mac, and merging it first lets it ride an alpha while the phone app is built.
2. The phone app joins your Mac and reads it. This covers the Xcode project under ios/Infinitary/, joining by link or Nearby, the phone's own key, the connection with catch-up, which Mac and whether it is in reach, the feed, a read-only list of cards, finding the Mac again, Leave and Removed. It also brings the test home, because that is this piece's test fixture. Checks: the published-contract client and the simulator tests on the Mac mini join the test home, and the captain's phone joins from Xcode. Needs 1, because today the strict join request refuses a system field as malformed (pairing.ts:916-917). Why apart: the trust part of the app gets its own review, and it is the base for 3, 4 and 5.
3. TestFlight puts each phone build on your phone. This is the dispatched workflow, with the simulator suite as its gate, then archive and upload with the App Store Connect key. Checks: the release tooling's own tests, and one real run delivering a build. Needs 2, plus the captain adding the key. Why apart: it holds the only release secret, and the key is a gate the captain controls.
4. Cards on the phone: answer, reply and close. Each card body draws in a web view, with the bridge, footer buttons, threads and past cards. Checks: the view journey's checks pass on the phone against the test home. Needs 2. Why apart: card scripts are the riskiest part of the app.
5. Talk and tasks from the phone. This is the message box, photos and dictation, plus the Tasks tab with records, search, Start, Continue, Steer and Interrupt, and notifications while the app is open. Checks: a typed message is the captain's own turn on the Mac, and a task started from the phone runs there. Needs 2. Why apart: it can be built at the same time as 3 and 4.
6. The phone app in the App Store. This is the sample for App Review, the listing, and the pinned review engine with its manifests and monitor. Checks: the engine's settings check, and a version going live after the captain merges its manifest. Needs 3, 4 and 5, plus the public beta's privacy and support pages after counsel. Why apart: it waits on counsel, and nothing else should wait with it.
Pieces 3, 4 and 5 can be built at the same time. Quillmark's Xcode project uses folder-synced groups, so new files rarely collide in the project file.

What changed from the plan's eight pieces:
- The test home folds into piece 2, because the rule never splits a change from its checks.
- Talk and Tasks join into one piece, because together they are one outcome and Talk alone is small.
- "+ A phone" with its code to scan comes out of the first Mac piece. The captain's FI3-681 pick was "the code arrives with the iPhone app", and the Devices design shows a phone chip only once the app exists.

The card asks one question: when the Mac shows "+ A phone". Option a puts it in piece 2, so the captain can scan from his first build, but people on the alpha would see it months before they can get the app. Option b puts it in piece 6, and the captain pastes the link once per phone until then. I recommend b, and an unanswered question takes b. Either way it stays six pieces.

Since the plan was written, the app was renamed. The phone app uses Infinitary names and the Mac app's id, com.getinfinitary.infinitary, still under team 9T2J7MNUP9. The old-name check would refuse the plan's Firstmate names. The contract is now at 8.5.0.

On "Start the next step", the first mate files the six pieces under INF-13, reuses INF-16 as piece 1, and links each piece only to the pieces it needs. I changed, committed and pushed nothing.
body:
Yes. INF-16 splits into six pieces under the plan's split rule, not one change and not the plan's eight. The first is a small change to your Mac, four build the phone app, and the last puts it in the App Store.

Six pieces, and what each one needs first

It cannot be one change, for one reason: the work reaches you through three separate gates. The last gate, App Review, also waits for counsel and the public pages, and nothing else should wait with it.

  1. Your Mac lets a phone join as a phone. A device that says it is a phone joins as a view, whichever link it used, so Projects never offers it under Runs on. While a phone is on its list, your Mac announces itself on your Wi-Fi, so the phone finds it again after its address changes. Nothing changes for anyone without a phone.

    Checks: pairing tests cover a phone that uses a computer's link. In the devices journey, a stand-in phone joins as a view. The announcement starts and stops with a phone on the list. The contract file is regenerated.
    Needs: nothing; it can start now.
    Why apart: pairing decides who may control your Mac, so it gets its own small review. Merged first, it can reach your Mac in an alpha while the phone app is built.

  2. The phone app joins your Mac and reads it. Infinitary for iPhone and iPad, installed from Xcode, joins with your Mac's link and asks you to confirm which Mac. Its key stays on this phone only. It stays connected, catches up after a drop, and shows which Mac and whether it is in reach. It shows the Activity feed and your cards as a read-only list. Nearby finds your Mac again after its address moves, and Leave and Removed work. It brings the test home: a stand-in Infinitary on the Mac mini with sample cards, feed lines and tasks.

    Checks: the published-contract client joins the test home and reads its cards. The phone's tests in the iPhone simulator on the Mac mini join it and show its feed and cards. Your phone joins your Mac from Xcode.
    Needs: 1. Until your Mac has piece 1, it refuses a phone that says it is a phone.
    Why apart: the phone's key and its pinned connection, the trust part of the app, get their own review. Pieces 3, 4 and 5 all build on it at the same time.

  3. TestFlight puts each phone build on your phone. A workflow you start with a version runs the phone's tests on the Mac mini, then archives and uploads the build with the App Store Connect key. The build reaches your phone through TestFlight.

    Checks: the release tooling's own tests run in the pull request checks. One real run puts a build on your phone.
    Needs: 2, and from you, the App Store Connect key in the repository's secrets.
    Why apart: it holds the only release secret and uploads to Apple, so its risk stays separate. You add the key at its gate.

  4. Cards on the phone: answer, reply and close. The card stack with its pager. Each body draws in a web view with the Mac's stylesheet, fonts, pictures and recordings, fitted to the width with pinch to zoom. Forms, a body's own buttons, footer buttons, close, the thread with reply, seen and past cards all work. A Settings or browser button says to do it on your Mac.

    Checks: the view journey's checks pass on the phone against the test home. An answer on the phone shows on the Mac, and out of reach refuses changes.
    Needs: 2.
    Why apart: card bodies run their own scripts inside the app, the riskiest part, so they get their own review.

  5. Talk and tasks from the phone. The message box, with the last turn above it, photos from the library as chips, and the keyboard's dictation. The Tasks tab lists tasks and opens each record with its timeline and crewmate. It searches, and offers Start, Continue, Steer and Interrupt. Notifications arrive while the app is open.

    Checks: a message typed on the phone is your own turn on the Mac. A task started from the phone runs on the Mac, and its record follows.
    Needs: 2.
    Why apart: it runs at the same time as 3 and 4, and keeps the cards review small.

  6. The phone app in the App Store. The built-in sample for App Review, the listing, icon and screenshots, and the pinned App Review engine with its manifests and monitor. It also links the privacy and support pages.

    Checks: the review engine's settings check runs in the pull request checks. A submitted version goes live after you merge its manifest.
    Needs: 3, 4 and 5. Outside the code, it waits for the public beta's privacy and support pages, after counsel, as you chose.
    Why apart: it waits on counsel, and none of the rest should wait with it.

What I changed from the plan's eight

Three of the plan's eight pieces failed the rule, and the drawing lights them.

The test home is the fixture piece 2's checks run on, and the rule never splits a change from its checks. Talk alone is small: the message box and dictation the keyboard already brings. Together with Tasks it is one outcome: give your first mate work and follow it. The Mac's code to scan cannot sit in piece 1, because piece 1 must be safe to stop at.

One question: when does your Mac show "+ A phone"?

The plan put "+ A phone", the code to scan, in the first Mac piece. That would show a code with no app to scan it. Your pick on FI3-681 was "Not yet: the link alone, and the code arrives with the iPhone app." The Devices design says the same: a phone chip joins only when the iPhone app exists.

I recommend b. The alpha reaches people who cannot get the phone app until the App Store. Under b, Nearby still lists your Mac from piece 2. Tapping it asks for the link until piece 6 brings the camera and the code. Either way it stays six pieces. A question left unanswered takes b.

When does your Mac show "+ A phone" with its code to scan?

Since the plan, the Mac app was renamed. Every piece uses Infinitary: the folder ios/Infinitary/, the name Infinitary, and the Mac app's own id, as your answer asked. Everything else in your saved answers stays as you chose it.

Start the next step files these six pieces under INF-13 with your answer, reusing INF-16 as piece 1. To keep it one change, or to move anything, reply here.

Evidence and exact names
  • The rule: the plan line in src/core/personal/sequencesSkill.ts (PLAN_STEP), and the feature sequence's pieces line: INF-16 is reused as piece 1, the rest are filed under INF-13, and each is blocked by exactly the pieces it needs, never by list order.
  • The accepted plan: FI3-1709 (task 976b2359), Save and defer with ten answers: direction A, in this project, a dispatched release, a sample plus a video for review, pages with the public beta, iPhone and iPad, iOS 18, the Mac app's id, fit to width, and Nearby as a guide with the code as the only way in.
  • Why piece 2 needs piece 1: pairRequestSchema in src/shared/connection.ts is strict and has no system field, so a join that sends one is refused as malformed (src/core/devices/pairing.ts lines 916-917); joinedKind (line 274) keeps the link's kind, so a phone with a computer's link joins as a computer today.
  • No Mac change is needed for pieces 4 and 5: the 44 requests with reach: "views" in src/shared/ipc.ts already cover cards (list, act, close, seen, thread, reply, picture, media, past), talk (converse, last turn) and tasks (board, detail, crewmate, search, run, steer, interrupt). Piece 4 may add a script that copies the card stylesheet, frame page and fonts into the phone build; it stays in piece 4 with the checks that use it.
  • Changed since the plan: PROTOCOL_VERSION is 8.5.0 (the plan read 7.0.0); electron-builder.yml names com.getinfinitary.infinitary, still team 9T2J7MNUP9; scripts/old-names.ts, run by pnpm check, refuses new Firstmate 3000 names, so the plan's ios/Firstmate/ becomes ios/Infinitary/.
  • The code to scan: FI3-681's saved answer qrcode = "Not yet: the link alone, and the code arrives with the iPhone app"; .claude/skills/infinitary-design/components/devices/DevicesTab.prompt.md: "A phone chip joins them only when the iPhone app exists." Alphas reach the community through the public tap (docs/alpha.md).
  • Parallel work: Quillmark's ios/Quillmark/Quillmark.xcodeproj/project.pbxproj uses folder-synced groups (PBXFileSystemSynchronizedRootGroup), so new files do not touch the project file; piece 2 sets the project up the same way, and pieces 3, 4 and 5 rarely collide.
  • Pull request checks for the phone: Quillmark's ci.yml runs only release-tooling tests on Linux, and its simulator suite (sim-suite.yml) is a release gate. Piece 3 carries the same, so pieces 2, 4 and 5 show their simulator runs in their pull requests.
  • New end-to-end journey cases are request-only in this project (docs/testing.md). The plan names one in piece 1 and one with "+ A phone"; filing the pieces carries that request.
  • Later, outside this plan, unchanged: notifications while the app is closed, Automations and Knowledge on the phone, the character, a side-by-side iPad layout, and the Secure Enclave for the phone's key.
  • I changed, committed and pushed nothing.
